source.title: SCANS: Mitigating the Exaggerated Safety for LLMs via Safety-Conscious Activation Steering
source.authors: Zou-Ying Cao; Yifei Yang; Hai Zhao

record.file_problem: None; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extracts harmful-minus-benign activation-difference vectors and intervenes on activations with them, reporting effects on refusal behavior. It tests a closely related vector-steering intervention, though not the original claim’s full ablation/addition procedure.
record.gate_note: The vectors are applied adaptively: the model is steered against the refusal vector for queries classified as benign and toward it for queries classified as harmful. Steering is at the last-token position in selected middle layers, not at every layer and position. The paper also reports classifier scores and layer/threshold/multiplier analyses; values used only to select layers or settings are not cataloged as results here.
record.test_reason: The study subtracts a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means vector at middle-layer last-token activations and reports the resulting refusal rates and capability. That bears on V1's causal claim, but by a different procedure: adaptive steering whose sign is set by a classifier, not all-layer directional ablation. It is a mitigation-method paper, and its refusal effects are entangled with classifier errors.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that SCANS sharply reduces false refusals on XSTest and OKTest (24.7% and 26.3% average decreases) while keeping refusal of harmful queries and largely preserving capability, with smaller capability costs in 13B than in 7B models. They note that classifier errors can slightly lower refusal on unsafe prompts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-benign activation differences, but applies adaptive steering at selected middle layers and only the last-token position. It does not perform all-layer/all-position ablation or the original direct addition test on harmless prompts.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with steering layers, multiplier α, classification threshold T, and classification layer set L. The paper reports that former-layer steering harms fluency and capability; threshold choice trades false refusals against adequate safety.

fits_no_version.finding: The similarity of hidden-state transitions to a harm reference classifies query harmfulness well: F1 0.911 on XSTest, second to GPT-4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-state transitions after appending an affirmative response separate harmful from benign queries.

record.problems: Results are averaged across 5 trials, but the paper does not report error bars or other uncertainty estimates in these tables. Refusal is primarily judged by predefined refusal-string matching, with a human comparison reported only graphically. Steering can reduce refusal on unsafe prompts, and capability losses are larger in some 7b settings.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted detailed per-model rows for some other safety metrics and the remaining Table 3 capability metrics (C4 perplexity and XSum ROUGE-1/2/L), as well as layer/threshold/multiplier sweep values. These are in Tables 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7; the core refusal outcomes and representative capability checks are included. Vicuna-13b adjacent Table 2 entries beyond XSTest were not cataloged because the flattened layout did not support confident assignment.

untested.parts: Not tested: removing refusal on harmful prompts (they are never steered against the direction); adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal (harmful queries are already at ceiling, and misclassified safe queries are not reported separately); all-layer, all-position ablation; a no-classifier steering condition.
No comparison of one direction against several.
Harm is classified from hidden-state transitions, but the study does not test whether harm is encoded separately from refusal.
No transfer of the direction across languages, variants or base-to-instruct models.

missing.what: Layer comparison: steering former layers destroys fluency (WikiText-2 perplexity 2946 for Llama2-7b). Middle layers reduce OKTest false refusal more than latter layers (0.33 vs 7.00).
Vocabulary projection: middle-layer directions promote refusal tokens (rejected, cannot, reject); former and latter layers do not.
Additional models on XSTest safe queries: Qwen1.5-32B 18.8 to 14.4 (OKTest 39.33 to 17.00); Llama3-8B-Instruct 13.6 to 4.0; Gemma2-9b-it 19.2 to 10.4.
vicuna-13b OKTest refusal 19.33 to 3.33, readable from Table 2 and omitted.
Large multiplier α=10 yields repetitive, degraded outputs, a capability cost of stronger steering.
OR-Bench-Hard safe-query refusal for Llama2-7b falls from 91.13 to 60.20, an incomplete reduction.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence for V1 comes only from subtracting the direction on queries classified benign, i.e. over-refused benign-looking prompts. It does not show that the direction mediates refusal of truly harmful prompts, or that adding it induces refusal: harmful-query rows are at ceiling and depend on the classifier. The refusal judge is string matching, checked against human judgement only in a figure. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate one direction at every layer and position, test adding it to harmless queries to induce refusal, or establish that it is the sole mediator. Tests adaptive addition/subtraction at selected middle layers and the resulting refusal and capability measures.
No weight edit or abliteration evaluation.
Does not test whether attacks suppress this direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Uses a hidden-state-transition similarity to classify query harmfulness, but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
Tests SCANS on several model variants, but does not test transfer of a direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training methods or timing.

relation.reason: Its own results measure how refusal rates and capability change when steering along or against the direction, compared with the unsteered model.

tranche.reason: Same difference-in-means direction (last token, AdvBench minus TruthfulQA, 64 each), but alpha-scaled addition/subtraction at middle layers (10-20 for 7B, 16-26 for 13B) with a classifier setting the sign. Not all-layer projection ablation. It reports refusal with versus without steering, so it bears on V1 by a different method. Not T1.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] ids, so l1-l3 follow pack order. Rows miss off-ceiling induction evidence: vicuna-7b Malicious 76.00 to 98.00 (Table 2); with T at 0.60, TruthfulQA refusal reaches 25.23 vs 5.05 default (Table 7). No random-direction control, effects are mixed up with classifier sigma(q) errors, and vicuna-7b alpha is tuned per dataset (Table 9).
